metadata.description: Learn ten possible kidney disease warning signs, who may be at higher risk and what blood, urine and imaging checks may involve.
metadata.title: 10 Warning Signs Your Kidneys May Be Struggling

landing.title: 10 Warning Signs Your Kidneys May Be Struggling
landing.intro: Some kidney changes are easy to miss. See which 10 warning signs deserve attention.

disclaimer: General educational information only. These signs do not prove that someone has kidney disease, and this guide is not a diagnosis or substitute for care from a qualified healthcare professional. Seek urgent medical care for new chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, confusion, a sudden major reduction in urine, or rapidly worsening swelling or illness.

sections.title: 10 Kidney Warning Signs
sections.intro: Early kidney disease often causes no symptoms, and these changes can have many other explanations. Blood and urine tests are the only way to assess how well the kidneys are working.

points.title: Urine that stays unusually foamy
paragraphs: Persistent foam or clusters of bubbles can sometimes occur when protein leaks into urine. Occasional bubbles may be harmless, but a repeated change can be checked with a simple urine albumin test.

points.title: Blood in your urine
paragraphs: Urine may look pink, red or brown, although blood can also be present without being visible. Infection, stones and other urinary conditions can cause bleeding too, so the cause needs proper assessment.

points.title: A lasting change in how often you urinate
paragraphs: Going more or less often than usual, waking repeatedly at night, or producing noticeably more or less urine can be worth discussing when the pattern is new or persistent.

points.title: Swelling around the ankles, feet, hands or eyes
paragraphs: Kidneys that cannot remove enough salt and fluid may contribute to swelling, called oedema. Puffiness around the eyes can also occur when substantial protein is being lost in urine.

points.title: Persistent tiredness or weakness
paragraphs: Reduced kidney function can allow waste products to build up and can contribute to anaemia. Both may cause unusual fatigue, weakness or reduced energy, but these symptoms have many possible causes.

points.title: Trouble concentrating or sleeping
paragraphs: Some people with advanced kidney disease report difficulty concentrating or disrupted sleep. Neither symptom is specific to the kidneys, so the wider pattern and test results matter.

points.title: Poor appetite, nausea or unexplained weight loss
paragraphs: A buildup of waste products in advanced kidney disease may affect appetite or cause nausea, vomiting and weight loss. New or persistent digestive symptoms should not be attributed to one condition without assessment.

points.title: Dry or persistently itchy skin
paragraphs: Kidney disease can disturb the balance of minerals and nutrients in the blood, which may contribute to dry or itchy skin. Skin conditions, allergies and medicines are among many other possible explanations.

points.title: Frequent muscle cramps
paragraphs: Changes in fluid, minerals or electrolytes can contribute to muscle cramps when kidney disease is advanced. Recurrent cramps still need context because activity, circulation and medicines can also play a part.

points.title: Shortness of breath or chest discomfort
paragraphs: Advanced kidney problems can contribute to fluid buildup, anaemia and heart complications, which may cause breathlessness or chest discomfort. New chest pain or severe breathing difficulty requires urgent medical care.

next.copy: Kidney disease often has no early symptoms, so diabetes, blood pressure and medical history can matter even more than how someone feels.

sections.title: Kidney Disease Risk: 10 Things Worth Knowing
sections.intro: Risk factors cannot diagnose kidney disease, but they can help determine who may benefit from regular blood and urine testing.

points.title: Diabetes
paragraphs: Diabetes is a leading cause of chronic kidney disease. High blood glucose over time can damage the kidneys' filtering units, which is why regular kidney checks are commonly recommended for people with diabetes.

points.title: High blood pressure
paragraphs: High blood pressure can damage blood vessels in the kidneys, and kidney disease can also make blood pressure harder to control. The relationship can work in both directions.

points.title: Heart and blood vessel disease
paragraphs: Heart disease, heart failure and other cardiovascular conditions are linked closely with kidney health. A clinician may consider both systems when deciding how often testing is needed.

points.title: A family history of kidney failure
paragraphs: Risk can be higher when a close relative has kidney failure or an inherited kidney condition. Tell a healthcare professional what condition affected the family and, if known, when it was diagnosed.

points.title: Getting older
paragraphs: Kidney function can decline with age, and chronic kidney disease becomes more common in older adults. Age alone does not establish a diagnosis, but it may influence testing decisions alongside other factors.

points.title: A previous acute kidney injury
paragraphs: Acute kidney injury is a sudden reduction in kidney function caused by illness, injury, dehydration or some medicines. Recovery is possible, but a previous episode can increase the risk of later chronic kidney problems.

points.title: Kidney stones, infections or urinary blockage
paragraphs: Repeated kidney stones, urinary infections or conditions that obstruct urine flow can sometimes affect the kidneys. An enlarged prostate is one possible cause of blockage in some people.

points.title: Autoimmune and inflammatory conditions
paragraphs: Conditions such as lupus and some forms of blood-vessel inflammation can affect kidney tissue. Monitoring depends on the specific disease, medicines and previous test results.

points.title: Medicines that may affect kidney function
paragraphs: Some medicines can affect the kidneys, particularly in certain doses, combinations or medical situations. Do not stop prescribed treatment on your own; ask a clinician or pharmacist whether monitoring is appropriate.

points.title: Risk is not a diagnosis
paragraphs: Someone can have several risk factors and normal kidney tests, while kidney disease can occur without an obvious risk factor. Testing—not a checklist—shows whether there is evidence of reduced function or kidney damage.

sections.title: What Kidney Blood And Urine Tests Actually Show
sections.intro: A kidney assessment combines history, blood pressure, blood tests and urine tests. Each measure answers a different question, and results are interpreted together.

points.title: Blood pressure
paragraphs: High blood pressure can both damage the kidneys and become harder to control when kidney function changes. A single reading may not represent the usual level, so repeated or home measurements can be useful.

points.title: Creatinine and eGFR
paragraphs: Creatinine is a waste product measured in blood. The result is used with personal information to estimate glomerular filtration rate, or eGFR—an estimate of how effectively the kidneys filter.

points.title: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
paragraphs: ACR or UACR checks whether albumin is leaking into urine. Persistent albumin can indicate kidney damage even when eGFR is relatively preserved, and the amount adds information about future risk.

points.title: Urine checks for blood, infection and other clues
paragraphs: Dipstick and laboratory tests can identify blood, protein, white cells and other findings. The pattern may suggest infection, stones, inflammation or another reason for investigation.

points.title: Repeat testing
paragraphs: Dehydration, acute illness, infection and medicines can temporarily alter results. Chronic kidney disease generally requires evidence that persists over time, unless the clinical situation shows an urgent acute problem.

points.title: Ultrasound, scans or biopsy when relevant
paragraphs: Imaging can assess kidney size and structure and look for cysts, stones or obstruction. A biopsy is used only in selected cases when examining kidney tissue could clarify the cause.

next.title: What Do Abnormal Kidney Results Mean?
next.copy: Some changes are temporary. Others point to chronic damage, acute injury, urinary blockage or a need for specialist review.

sections.title: What Abnormal Kidney Results Can Mean
sections.intro: An abnormal result needs context: previous measurements, current illness, urine findings, medicines and the speed of change all affect what happens next.

points.title: A temporary change from dehydration or illness
paragraphs: Vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or reduced fluid intake can alter kidney blood tests. Clinicians assess the cause and decide how urgently the result should be repeated.

points.title: Acute kidney injury
paragraphs: A rapid decline over hours or days is different from long-term chronic kidney disease. Infection, low blood pressure, obstruction and some medicines are among possible causes, and urgent treatment may be needed.

points.title: Persistently reduced eGFR
paragraphs: A lower eGFR that remains abnormal over at least three months may support a diagnosis of chronic kidney disease. The exact stage and trend matter more than one isolated number.

points.title: Albumin or protein in urine
paragraphs: Persistent albumin suggests damage to the kidney filters and adds information about risk. Diabetes, high blood pressure and other kidney conditions can contribute.

points.title: Blood in urine
paragraphs: Infection, stones, prostate or bladder conditions and kidney disease can all cause blood. Visible blood or a persistent laboratory finding needs assessment rather than being assumed to come from CKD.

points.title: A urinary blockage
paragraphs: Stones, an enlarged prostate or another obstruction can prevent urine draining normally. Imaging and prompt treatment may protect kidney function.

points.title: A medicine-related effect
paragraphs: Some medicines can alter kidney function or electrolytes, especially during illness or in combinations. Do not stop prescribed treatment independently; the clinician can review dose, monitoring and alternatives.

points.title: Complications that need treatment
paragraphs: Advanced CKD can contribute to anaemia, mineral and bone problems, fluid overload and abnormal potassium or acid balance. Additional tests identify which complications are present.

points.title: A need for specialist referral
paragraphs: Rapid decline, substantial albumin, difficult blood pressure, unusual urine findings, advanced stages or uncertainty about the cause may prompt referral to a kidney specialist.

points.title: A monitoring and protection plan
paragraphs: The plan may include repeat tests, blood-pressure and diabetes treatment, medicines that protect kidney function, lifestyle advice and a schedule based on both eGFR and ACR.

sections.title: Kidney Disease Stages: What Really Matters
sections.intro: The NHS groups eGFR from G1 to G5 and urine albumin from A1 to A3. A stage is useful, but it must be read alongside albumin, trend, cause and overall health.

points.title: G1: eGFR above 90 with other evidence of damage
paragraphs: A normal-looking filtration estimate does not exclude CKD when persistent albumin, structural changes or another marker of kidney damage is present.

points.title: G2: eGFR 60 to 89 with other evidence of damage
paragraphs: A mildly reduced estimate is not labelled CKD on its own. Other persistent evidence and the clinical context are required.

points.title: G3a: eGFR 45 to 59
paragraphs: This represents a mild-to-moderate reduction. Many people have few symptoms, but cardiovascular risk, urine albumin and change over time influence monitoring.

points.title: G3b: eGFR 30 to 44
paragraphs: The reduction is more marked and complications become more relevant. Medicine doses, blood pressure, albumin and referral criteria may need closer review.

points.title: G4: eGFR 15 to 29
paragraphs: This is advanced CKD. Specialist care commonly addresses complications and discusses future treatment options in case kidney function continues to decline.

points.title: G5: eGFR below 15
paragraphs: This means the kidneys have lost most of their filtering function. Some people need dialysis or a transplant, while care is individualised around symptoms, health and preferences.

points.title: A1 to A3: why urine albumin changes the picture
paragraphs: Higher ACR categories indicate more albumin in urine and generally greater kidney and cardiovascular risk. Someone with a higher eGFR but substantial albumin may still need active treatment and monitoring.

points.title: The trend may matter as much as today's stage
paragraphs: Stable results and a rapid fall can carry very different implications even within the same category. Clinicians compare previous tests rather than interpreting the latest number in isolation.

points.title: The cause and complications matter
paragraphs: Inherited disease, diabetes, inflammation or obstruction can follow different paths. Potassium, anaemia, fluid status, blood pressure and bone health add further context.

points.title: Statistics and stages cannot predict one person
paragraphs: Many people live a long time with CKD and most do not progress to kidney failure. The clinical team can explain individual risk using the full pattern of results.

conclusion.copy: Kidney disease is often found through testing before symptoms appear. eGFR, urine albumin, the direction of change and the underlying cause are considered together—one number is never the whole story.
